title: Loops
summary: A loop repeats instructions so you do not have to write them again.

subtopics.title: for
subtopics.explanation: A `for` loop repeats while its condition remains true. It commonly has a starting value, a check, and an update. It is like counting pages until reaching the last one. Make the update move toward the stopping condition to avoid an infinite loop. For example, a for loop can count through the indexes of a short array. In practice, a for loop can visit each index when an item’s position is needed.

subtopics.title: for...of
subtopics.explanation: `for...of` visits each value in an array or another iterable. It is like reading every item from a list in order. Use it when you need the values but not the numeric index. If you need both, another iteration method may make the relationship clearer. For example, use for-of to read each task object when its index is irrelevant. In practice, use for-of to read task objects when their indexes do not matter.

subtopics.title: while
subtopics.explanation: A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is true. It is useful when the number of repetitions is not known in advance. It is like continuing to stir until a mixture reaches the right consistency. Change the condition’s inputs so the loop can finish. For example, a while loop can retry while a response is unavailable, but include a limit or exit. In practice, update the condition’s value inside a while loop so it can stop.

subtopics.title: break and continue
subtopics.explanation: `break` exits the current loop; `continue` skips the rest of this repetition and moves to the next one. It is like leaving a queue or skipping one item. Use them when they clarify the logic, but avoid control flow that makes the loop hard to follow. For example, use continue to skip completed records only when that keeps the loop clear. In practice, continue can skip one invalid row while processing later rows.

subtopics.title: Stopping safely
subtopics.explanation: Check that every loop can reach its stopping condition. A loop that never changes its condition can freeze the page. It is like a checklist that keeps restarting without crossing off an item. Test empty lists and boundary values as well as ordinary cases. For example, test a loop with an empty list and a list containing one item. In practice, test the loop with no items, one item, and several items.

foundations.overview: A loop repeats code while it visits values or a condition remains true. Loops are useful for processing lists and repeating a task. Think of them like following each step on a checklist. Choose the loop form that makes the stopping rule obvious, and ensure every repeating path can eventually stop.
foundations.whyItMatters: Iteration is central to processing lists and repeated work. Clear stop conditions and edge-case checks prevent frozen pages and off-by-one mistakes.
foundations.browserPerspective: JavaScript runs on a single thread, so a long-running or infinite loop blocks the main thread: the page cannot paint, scroll, or respond to clicks until the loop finishes. That is why tight loops over huge data sets can freeze the UI and why the browser may warn about an unresponsive script.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Building HTML for a list of products, summing items in a cart, searching an array for a match, retrying a request until it succeeds, and stepping through characters of a string are all everyday loop tasks.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct, efficient loops keep interfaces responsive and data accurate; a bug like an off-by-one error or an accidental infinite loop can corrupt results or freeze the app, directly hurting users.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Choosing the right loop (for index control, for...of for values, for...in for keys) makes code clearer and less bug-prone, and understanding break/continue avoids tangled boolean flags.
foundations.performanceImpact: Loop choice and body cost dominate hot paths. Doing expensive work (DOM updates, allocations) inside a loop instead of batching it is a top cause of jank; minimizing work per iteration keeps loops fast.
commonUseCases: Iterating an array to render or transform each item
Summing, counting, or searching through a collection
Repeating an action a fixed number of times
Reading object key/value pairs to build output

commonMisconceptions.myth: for...in is the way to loop over arrays.
commonMisconceptions.reality: for...in iterates keys as strings and can include inherited properties; for arrays use for...of, forEach, or a plain for loop to get values in order.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can break out of forEach with break or return.
commonMisconceptions.reality: break is a syntax error in forEach and return only ends the current callback; to stop early, use a for/for...of loop or methods like some/find.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A loop with no visible counter cannot become infinite.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A while loop can repeat forever if its condition never changes.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Break and continue improve every loop.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Extra exits can obscure the path; use them only when they make the intent clearer.

visualExplorer.title: How a for loop executes step by step
visualExplorer.caption: Watch the three parts of a for loop run in order across each iteration.

config.intro: Follow `for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++)` as it counts from 0 to 2 and then stops.

steps.name: Initialize
steps.detail: The initializer `let i = 0` runs exactly once, before the loop body.

steps.name: Check condition
steps.detail: The condition `i < 3` is evaluated. If true, the body runs; if false, the loop ends.

steps.name: Run the body
steps.detail: The statements inside { } execute for the current value of i.

steps.name: Update
steps.detail: The update `i++` runs after the body, increasing i by 1.

steps.name: Re-check and repeat
steps.detail: Control returns to the condition; this repeats until `i < 3` becomes false.

steps.name: Exit
steps.detail: When i reaches 3 the condition is false, so the loop stops and code after it runs.

interactiveExamples.title: Counting with a for loop
interactiveExamples.explanation: A simple for loop prints numbers 1 through 5. Change the condition or update to see how the count shifts.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Number 1 through Number 5 logged to the console.

interactiveExamples.title: for...of vs for...in
interactiveExamples.explanation: for...of gives you the values of an array; for...in gives you the keys of an object. Notice how each is suited to its data shape.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: value: apple, value: banana, then name => Ada, role => dev.

interactiveExamples.title: break and continue in action
interactiveExamples.explanation: continue skips odd numbers; break stops the loop once we pass 8. This shows how to control which iterations run.

codeLab.title: Sum the numbers in an array
codeLab.instructions: Write a loop that adds up every number in the `nums` array and stores the result in `total`. Use any loop you like, then log the total.
hints: Start total at 0 before the loop.
Use for...of to read each value, then add it to total with +=.

keyTakeaways: A `for` loop repeats while its condition remains true.
A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is true.
`break` exits the current loop; `continue` skips the rest of this repetition and moves to the next one.
Check that every loop can reach its stopping condition.
